why_not_production: The only deployed environment, readypick-pilot, holds three tenants and thirty jobs and ZERO candidates, profiles, applications and reports (docs/verification/AI_UPGRADE_BASELINE.md, 2026-09-09). context_chunks holds zero rows because services/rag/index.index_document has no caller. A production corpus therefore cannot be drawn, and this corpus is hand authored so the retrieval metrics have a fixed corpus to hold constant, which is the BrowseComp-Plus idea W7.1 is built on. It is NOT a production sample and no case in this set claims to be.

chunks.text: Backend Engineer, payments. Must have production Kafka experience and be able to reason about consumer group rebalancing under partition change.
Nice to have: exposure to Postgres logical replication and to schema migrations executed without downtime.
Behavioural: the engineer is expected to raise a risk before it becomes an incident rather than after.
Reduced payment settlement lag from nineteen minutes to under four by resizing the Kafka consumer group and pinning partition assignment to the settlement key.
Strong team player with a proven track record of delivering high quality software in fast paced environments.
Ran a Postgres major version upgrade across eleven databases using logical replication, with a documented cutover and a tested rollback.
Familiar with distributed systems, microservices, cloud platforms and modern engineering practices.
When the consumer group stalled we found the rebalance was triggered by a slow poll rather than by a broker failure, so we raised max poll interval and cut the batch size.
I flagged the replication lag to the on call channel two days before the release because the write volume was already tracking above what we had load tested.
Public repository: a partition assignor implementation with property tests covering rebalance under broker restart and under consumer restart.
Public repository: a migration runner that refuses a migration lacking a down step, with a test suite exercising interrupted migrations.
Former platform lead confirms the settlement latency work was owned end to end by this engineer and that the rollback plan was exercised in staging.
Expert in Kafka, Kubernetes, Terraform, Go, Rust, Python, TypeScript, GraphQL and machine learning.
I have not used logical replication myself. I have read the runbook for it and I would want a second pair of eyes the first time.
Wrote the incident review for a four hour payment outage, including the two contributing changes and the detection gap that let it run for ninety minutes.
The hardest part was telling the product owner that the date was wrong. I brought the revised estimate and the two things I had cut, not just the bad news.
Engineering Manager, platform. Must have run a team through a reorganisation while keeping delivery commitments visible and honest.
Nice to have: has built a hiring loop and can describe how it changed the shape of the team.
Behavioural: gives a direct report difficult feedback early rather than letting it accumulate to a review cycle.
Merged two platform teams of six and four, kept the roadmap public through the merge, and lost one person over eight months against a company average of three.
Passionate people leader focused on empowering teams to deliver world class outcomes.
Rebuilt the backend hiring loop around a paired debugging exercise, cutting time to offer from forty one days to twenty three across nineteen hires.
I told him in the first week that the design reviews were not landing, gave him two specific examples, and we agreed a check in every Friday rather than waiting for the cycle.
During the merge I published the delivery dates I believed rather than the ones I had been given, and I said which two I expected to miss.
The hiring loop change was mostly my manager's idea. My part was running the calibration sessions and writing the rubric.
The previous director confirms the two team merge and that attrition through it was one person, and adds that the roadmap was published weekly throughout.
Public write up: the paired debugging exercise used in the hiring loop, with the rubric and the calibration notes.
Managed large cross functional teams and drove significant improvements in velocity and morale.
I have never run a reorganisation. I have been through two as a lead and I watched how the second one handled the people who were reassigned.
Introduced a weekly written delivery note naming what slipped and why, which the two teams kept using after the merge closed.
The feedback I regret is the one I saved for the review. By then he had repeated it four times and it read as an ambush.
VP Engineering. Must have owned a multi year platform migration with a stated cost and a stated benefit, both measured after the fact.
Nice to have: has run an engineering budget through a contraction and can name what was protected and what was cut.
Behavioural: publishes a decision that later proved wrong together with what the decision rested on.
Led a three year migration off a shared monolith database, measured at fourteen engineer years spent against a reduction in change failure rate from eleven percent to three.
Held headcount flat through a nineteen percent budget reduction by ending two internal tools programmes and moving their owners onto the migration.
Visionary technology leader with a track record of driving transformational change at scale.
The build versus buy call on the feature store was wrong. We spent eleven months on it and I wrote up the two assumptions that did not hold, one of which I had been warned about.
In the contraction I protected the on call rotation and the migration, and I cut the internal developer portal, which was the thing I personally wanted most.
The former chief executive confirms the migration ran three years, confirms the change failure numbers were reported to the board quarterly, and confirms the feature store write up was circulated.
Published conference talk with the migration's cost model, including the engineer year accounting and what it excluded.
Responsible for engineering strategy, architecture, delivery, hiring, culture, security and vendor relationships.
I did not own the budget. I proposed the reductions and the chief financial officer decided which of them happened.
Ran a quarterly written review naming every architectural decision reversed that quarter and the evidence that reversed it.
The migration's benefit case rested on change failure rate, and I would use lead time instead now, because change failure rate moved partly for reasons the migration did not cause.
Chief Technology Officer. Must have carried a technology position into a board decision that went against the executive team's preference.
Nice to have: has taken a company through a regulated audit of its data handling.
Behavioural: separates what the company knows from what it believes when reporting to a board.
Argued against the proposed acquisition of a data vendor on integration grounds, lost the first vote, and was asked to run the integration review that reversed it four months later.
Took the company through its first external audit of candidate data handling, closing eleven findings of which three required a schema change.
Seasoned executive with deep expertise across the technology landscape and a passion for innovation.
I told the board we had one quarter of evidence and three quarters of assumption, and I labelled which of the four numbers on the slide was which.
The audit found we were retaining raw assessment media past what the consent covered. We deleted it and changed the pipeline so deletion happens after the verification, not before it.
The board chair confirms the acquisition position was carried against the executive team's preference and that the integration review was commissioned as a result.
Published post on separating measured from assumed numbers in a board pack, with the template the company adopted.
Board level technology leadership including strategy, governance, risk, compliance and organisational design.
I was not in the room for the audit close. My head of data ran it and I read the findings afterwards.
Losing the first vote was the right outcome for the process even though I thought the decision was wrong, and I said so at the time rather than afterwards.
Instituted a board reporting standard in which every figure carries its source and its measurement window, adopted across three functions.
Recognised thought leader in artificial intelligence, cloud transformation and data driven decision making.
Data Platform Engineer. Must have production Airflow experience: authoring DAGs, backfills, and on-call ownership of failed runs.
Nice to have for the data platform role: dbt model refactoring and exposure to Spark structured streaming.
Behavioural expectation: the engineer documents a pipeline before handing it over and flags data-quality regressions to the owning analyst first.
Cut the nightly warehouse build from six hours to ninety minutes by splitting one monolithic Airflow DAG into eleven task groups with per-table sensors.
Migrated one hundred and forty dbt models to contract-checked schemas; downstream dashboard breakage reports fell to zero over the following quarter.
Passionate about big data and modern data stacks. Familiar with all major pipeline tools.
Wrote a Spark job that deduplicated the clickstream table at four billion rows a day, holding executor memory under the cluster ceiling.
When the backfill double-counted revenue I stopped the DAG, wrote the idempotency key into the merge, and re-ran the affected partitions only. The finance report was correct by the Monday close.
I have not used Spark streaming in production. My streaming work was Kafka consumers writing to the warehouse in micro-batches.
I raised the schema drift with the analyst who owned the model before touching it, because a silent fix would have moved her numbers without her knowing.
Reference check, former lead: he owned the Airflow estate for two years and his backfills were the ones nobody had to re-run.
GitHub project: an open-source dbt package for slowly changing dimensions, forty-one stars, used by two companies I know of.
Android Engineer, consumer app. Must have Kotlin and Jetpack Compose in production; crash-free sessions above ninety-nine point five percent is the bar.
Nice to have: Play Store staged rollouts, baseline profiles, and startup-time tracing.
Took the checkout screen from XML views to Compose behind a feature flag; scroll jank on low-end devices fell by half as measured in the vitals dashboard.
Reduced cold start from three point two seconds to one point four by deferring three SDK initialisations and adding a baseline profile.
Android enthusiast since university. Strong knowledge of the full Android ecosystem.

The crash was a coroutine cancelled mid-write to DataStore. I reproduced it with a turbine test, moved the write into a NonCancellable block, and the crash rate for that screen went to zero in the next release.
I have never shipped a staged rollout myself; releases at my company went to one hundred percent in one step and the platform team owned the button.
I profiled the startup trace before touching anything, because the slow frame everyone blamed was not the one the trace showed.
Play Console vitals attached to the application: crash-free sessions ninety-nine point seven percent across the last three releases.
Side project APK included: a habit tracker in Compose with a widget, published under my own developer account.
Engineering Manager, platform team. Must have run an incident process: postmortems that produce owned actions, not documents.
Nice to have: experience forecasting delivery with historical cycle-time data rather than story points.
Behavioural: the manager gives corrective feedback within the week, not at the review.
Rebuilt the on-call rotation for a nine-person team: paging volume fell forty percent in two quarters, tracked in the incident tool, and no engineer left the team that year.
Ran forty-one postmortems over two years; the repeat-incident rate for causes with a named owner fell to one in ten.
Servant leader who believes people are the real product. Experienced in all aspects of engineering management.

One engineer was missing every estimate. I sat with him through a week of work, found the interruptions were review requests from another team, moved that queue, and his throughput recovered without a performance plan.
I told the director the migration would slip two sprints the day I knew, with the cycle-time data that said so, and offered the cut list rather than a heroic promise.
I have not run a formal hiring loop end to end; my last company had a central recruiting function that owned the process and I only interviewed.
Upward feedback excerpt, verified: three of four direct reports named his postmortem facilitation as the thing they would keep.
Introduced cycle-time forecasting; the last six quarterly commitments landed within one sprint of the forecast.

When two seniors both wanted the tech-lead seat I split the domain by service boundary, wrote the split down, and revisited it with them after a quarter. One of them still disagrees, and the team shipped.
Sales Operations Manager. Must have owned CRM pipeline hygiene: stage definitions, exit criteria, and a forecast the CFO can stand behind.
Nice to have: commission plan modelling and territory rebalancing.
Rewrote the pipeline stages with exit criteria the reps agreed to; forecast accuracy moved from plus-minus forty percent to plus-minus twelve over three quarters.
Rebalanced fourteen territories using two years of closed-won data; the bottom quartile of reps closed the gap to median by a third.
Results-driven revenue operations professional with a passion for data.

The forecast was inflated because stale opportunities never died. I added a ninety-day no-activity sweep that moved them to a parking stage the forecast ignores, and told sales leadership exactly what would disappear before I ran it.
I have no experience with commission modelling; finance owned the plan at both my companies and I supplied the attainment data.
Verified by the former CRO in writing: forecast accuracy figures as stated, and she would rehire him.
I trained the reps on the new stages myself, one pod at a time, because a memo would have changed the fields and not the behaviour.
Head of Design. Must have built and scaled a design system that product teams actually adopted, and grown a team through at least one reorganisation.
Nice to have: design research practice built from nothing; pricing-page experimentation experience.
Behavioural: defends craft quality in the roadmap conversation without becoming the blocker the roadmap routes around.
Grew design from four to nineteen across three product lines; regretted attrition over three years was two people, both relocations.
Shipped the design system to eighty percent component adoption in eighteen months, measured by automated audit of the production bundles.
Award-winning design leader passionate about user-centred everything.
Two product teams forked the button. I did not mandate; I sat both leads down with the audit numbers, agreed one owner, and put a deprecation date on the fork. Adoption is how you know it worked.
I have never built a research practice from zero; I inherited two researchers and scaled from there, which is a different problem.
When the CEO wanted the redesign in half the time I put the two cut options on one page, priced in support tickets, and let him choose with the cost visible.
Reference, former CPO: the design system claim is real, and the adoption number matches what our tooling reported.
Ran the reorganisation from platform-aligned to journey-aligned squads; time-to-first-design-review halved.
VP Engineering. Must have led a platform migration measured in years, not sprints, and negotiated the vendor contracts under it.
Nice to have: an engineering brand people cite when they apply; a budget line survived through a downturn.
Led the datacentre-to-cloud migration of two hundred services over twenty-six months, with the parallel-run bill capped and published monthly to the board.
Renegotiated the observability contract at renewal: forty percent unit-cost reduction against the prior term, with an exit clause we later used.
Visionary technology executive with a track record of transformation at scale.

Halfway through the migration the vendor deprecated the instance family we had sized for. I froze new movement for a month, re-benchmarked, and burned the contingency I had defended in the original plan. We landed four weeks late and inside budget.
I have not carried a budget through a downturn; my tenure was all growth years and the cuts happened after I left.
I publish the postmortem of my own decisions once a quarter to the whole org, including the one where my build-versus-buy call cost us a year.
Board minutes excerpt, verified: the migration cost tracking was presented monthly as described.
Two of my staff engineers keynoted industry conferences on work we open-sourced; both cite it in their hiring funnels.
The hardest call was stopping the second datacentre exit halfway to fund the security remediation. I made the trade explicit to both teams rather than letting the roadmap quietly absorb it.
Chief Financial Officer. Must have taken a company through an external audit cycle with zero material findings, and owned treasury policy.
Nice to have: fundraising across at least two instruments; transfer-pricing exposure.
Behavioural: tells the board the bad number the week it is known.
Closed four consecutive annual audits with no material weakness; the one significant deficiency in year one was remediated and retested within the same cycle.
Rewrote treasury policy after a counterparty scare: diversified across three banks with exposure ceilings, board-ratified, and stress-tested quarterly.
Strategic finance leader and trusted business partner to CEOs.
We found the revenue recognition error ourselves in month ten. I took it to the audit committee before the auditors found it, with the restatement quantified and the control fix already running.
I have not led a debt raise; both my raises were equity and the venture debt line predated me.
When the CEO wanted the aggressive booking treatment I wrote him the memo saying no with the accounting literature attached, and I kept a copy.
Audit partner reference, verified: four clean opinions as stated, and the committee minutes reflect the self-reported restatement.
Raised a Series C and a venture debt extension in the same year; the debt covenants have never been within twenty percent of breach.
I brief the board on cash runway monthly with the same model finance uses internally, because two models is how surprises happen.
Chief Product Officer. Must have run a product portfolio through a deliberate kill decision: sunset a line, keep the customers.
Nice to have: a discovery practice the sales team quotes; pricing migration at scale.
Sunset the legacy reporting product over fourteen months: ninety-two percent of its revenue migrated to the replacement, with churn from the sunset itself under three percent.
Built the discovery practice: every funded bet now carries recorded customer evidence, and the two bets that failed last year failed in discovery, not in build.
Product visionary obsessed with customer delight and outcomes over outputs.
The kill decision was mine to recommend. I put the maintenance cost, the migration path, and the churn model on one page, and I told the two biggest customers myself before the announcement.
I have never run a pricing migration; pricing sat with the CRO at my last two companies and I supplied the packaging.

When the board pushed the AI feature for the earnings narrative I shipped a scoped assistant with a measured activation target instead of the platform rewrite they described, and I said so in the deck.
Reference, former CEO: the sunset numbers are accurate and the customer calls happened as described.
Introduced quarterly portfolio reviews where every line owner argues the kill case for their own product before arguing the invest case.
Discovery evidence is recorded interviews and usage cohorts, not opinion decks; I rejected a funded bet from my own favourite team for arriving without either.
Behavioural expectation for the CPO: disagrees with the CEO in the room and commits outside it.
Attached portfolio one-pager: the kill-case template used in quarterly reviews, redacted.
